description:
Hi! I'm Fanny, a 5th-year Aerospace Engineering student at IPSA, France, specializing in Space Systems, Launchers and Satellites.

I'm passionate about space exploration and would love to develop an innovative solution for Lunar Landing Site Navigator, helping identify and evaluate potential lunar landing sites.

Let's combine our skills and build something amazing for lunar exploration! 🌙🚀
summary:
SELENE: From Lunar Surface Analysis to Mission Design

SELENE is a web application that turns a lunar landing site and a date into clear, checkable answers. Will the site be lit? Will Earth be in view? Is the ground safe? Can a spacecraft get there in time? The user picks a site near the lunar south pole and a date. SELENE then uses NASA/NAIF SPICE ephemerides to compute where the Sun and Earth sit in the local sky, and derives illumination and direct-to-Earth communication windows. It also ranks 8,781 candidate sites by slope using LRO/LOLA elevation data and checks a planned surface stay against go/no-go limits. Going beyond the challenge, SELENE links the site to a mission: it computes an Earth–Moon transfer and a powered descent, then replays them in a 3D Sun–Earth–Moon view. Our geometry matches an independent JPL Horizons reference to better than 0.01″ in azimuth.

This matters because at the south pole, where Artemis is heading, the Sun and Earth stay close to the horizon. A few hundred metres of relief can mean days of darkness and silence. Our demo scenario showed exactly that: the landing came 2.5 days after sunset, with Earth below the horizon. Separate tools hide this kind of link between site, date and trajectory; SELENE shows it.
details: SELENE is a web platform for planning a landing at the lunar south pole. The user picks a site and a date. SELENE uses NASA SPICE ephemerides and LRO/LOLA elevation data to compute Sun and Earth visibility, communication windows and terrain slopes, and checks a surface stay against go/no-go limits. A scenario can be saved as a mission. SELENE then computes the Earth–Moon transfer and descent and replays them in a 3D Sun–Earth–Moon view. Its main benefit is to bring together questions that normally need separate expert tools, with precise results (better than 0.01″ against JPL Horizons) and each result's source shown. We built it with a C++17 science service (CSPICE), a Rust/Axum gateway, a React/TypeScript/Three.js frontend and a Python trajectory engine ported to C++, deployed with Docker and GitHub Actions. What makes it creative is the link from landing site to full mission. Our demo showed that a reachable trajectory could land in darkness, with Earth out of view. The team focused on the harsh polar geometry, labelling how reliable each result is, and keeping it easy to use for non-specialists.
